title: Lesson 16 - A3 Legal Responsibilities
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: What must organisations do by law to protect personal data?

sections.heading: Flying start (warm-up)
sections.text: Recap from A1 and A2, then think ahead. Try each one before reading the answer.
points: 1. One internal and one external threat? E.g. internal: a disgruntled employee or accidental data loss. External: a hacker or a phishing attack
2. A company is fined after a data breach. Which type of loss? Financial loss (the fine is legal liability)
3. True or false: "Risk acceptance means an organisation decides to live with a risk instead of reducing it." True
4. Which UK organisation publishes reports and advisories on current cyber threats? The NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre)

5. Think ahead: name three organisations that hold personal data about you (e.g. your school, your GP, your phone network). What should they NOT be allowed to do with it? E.g. sell it, share it without a reason, or keep it forever
Today's focus: what UK GDPR and the Computer Misuse Act 1990 require organisations to do with personal data. Next (A4): the security measures organisations use to meet these duties

sections.heading: Personal data (PII)
sections.text: Personal data is any information that can identify a living person, on its own or combined with other data. PII means personally identifying information.
points: Examples: name, home address, email, date of birth, bank details, photo, medical notes, IP address
Data laws apply to every organisation
They cover data in storage and when it is transferred
They cover the privacy of PII
They cover unauthorised access to computers and devices
They cover unauthorised access to data, and changes to data

sections.heading: Two key laws you need to know

head: UK GDPR + DPA 2018
Computer Misuse Act 1990 (CMA)
rows: Controls how organisations collect, store, use and share personal data
Makes it a crime to access or change computer material without permission
Gives people rights over their data
Protects data from unauthorised access and modification
Enforced by the ICO: fines up to £17.5m or 4% of turnover
Organisations must take due care to stop unauthorised access

points: Remember: GDPR = the rules for handling data. CMA = the crime of breaking in

diagram.alt: Left: UK GDPR with the Data Protection Act 2018 sets the rules for handling personal data. Collect it with a lawful basis and only what you need (data minimisation). Use it fairly and openly, and only for the stated purpose (purpose limitation). Store it accurately and not for too long (storage limitation). Protect it (integrity and confidentiality). It is enforced by the ICO, with fines up to 17.5 million pounds or 4% of turnover. Right: the Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes breaking in a crime. An attacker getting into an organisation's system without permission commits a criminal offence: unauthorised access, access to commit a further crime, impairing a computer or data, or making or supplying hacking tools. The organisation must take due care to stop unauthorised access, for example MFA, patching and disabling leavers' accounts.
diagram.caption: GDPR = the rules for handling data. CMA = the crime of breaking in.

sections.heading: The 7 UK GDPR principles
sections.text: All seven are compulsory. Learn the name, what it means and a breach.

head: Principle
What it means
Example of a breach
rows: 1. Lawfulness
Must have a valid legal reason (lawful basis) to use the data
A fitness app shares users' location history with advertisers with no lawful basis
2. Fairness and transparency
Treat people fairly and be open about what is collected and why
A quiz app secretly copies users' phone contacts
3. Purpose limitation (limited to stated purposes)
Only use data for the purpose you told people
A school uses parents' emergency contact numbers to send fundraising texts
4. Accuracy
Keep data correct and up to date; fix mistakes quickly
A GP surgery records the wrong allergy and doesn't fix it when told
5. Data minimisation (keep the minimum amount of data)
Only collect data you actually need
A cinema asks for your National Insurance number to book a ticket
6. Storage limitation (store for the minimum time)
Don't keep data longer than needed
A recruitment agency keeps rejected applicants' CVs for 15 years
7. Integrity and confidentiality
Keep data secure from unauthorised access, loss or damage
An unencrypted laptop of patient records is left on a train

points: Common mix-up: purpose limitation = WHAT you do with data; data minimisation = HOW MUCH you collect

sections.heading: Worked example: spotting a breach
sections.text: SnapPrint, an online photo printer, asks customers for their name, address, email and date of birth. It keeps all photos and details forever, even after orders are delivered.
points: Step 1, underline the evidence: "keeps … forever, even after orders are delivered"
Step 2, match it to a principle: storage limitation
Step 3, explain using the scenario: it breaches storage limitation because it keeps details forever, even though it no longer needs them after delivery
A second breach: data minimisation, because a date of birth isn't needed to print photos
Quick check (a): a hospital keeps patient records on a database with no password → integrity and confidentiality
Quick check (b): a takeaway app asks for your mother's maiden name to order a pizza → data minimisation
Quick check (c): a bank keeps writing to your old address after you told them you moved → accuracy

sections.heading: The 6 lawful bases for processing data
sections.text: A lawful basis is the legal reason for using personal data. Organisations must pick one before they start, and tell people.

head: Lawful basis
In plain English
Example
rows: Consent
The person has freely and clearly agreed
A photographer asks parents' permission before posting school play photos
Contractual obligation
Needed to deliver a contract
A mobile network uses your bank details to take your monthly payment
Legitimate interest
A genuine business reason that doesn't override people's rights
A college uses CCTV in its car park to keep people safe
Vital interest
Needed to protect someone's life
A school shares a pupil's allergy details with A&E
Legal requirement
The law requires it
An employer keeps staff right-to-work documents, as the law requires
Public interest
Needed for an official or public task
The DVLA uses driver details to issue driving licences

points: Myth: organisations always need your consent. Reality: consent is only 1 of 6 lawful bases
Myth: legitimate interest covers anything that makes money. Reality: it must not override people's rights
Myth: a pre-ticked box counts as consent. Reality: consent must be a clear, active choice
Quick check: a gym takes your bank details to collect your monthly membership fee → contractual obligation

sections.heading: Your personal rights under UK GDPR
sections.text: People have six rights over their data. Organisations must usually respond within one month. Tip: look for the verb: see, be told, fix, stop, move, human check?

head: Right
What it lets you do
rows: Right of access
See a copy of your data (a Subject Access Request)
Right to be informed
Be told how and why your data is used
Right to have data corrected, removed or restricted
Fix it, delete it or pause its use
Right to object
Say "stop", e.g. to direct marketing
Right to data portability
Get your data in a machine-readable format
Right not to be subject to automated decision-making
Ask for a human to review a decision

points: Amira leaves a social network and asks it to delete all her posts → corrected, removed or restricted
An algorithm sets Leo's insurance quote and he asks for a person to check it → automated decision-making
Priya asks her old bank for her history in a file her new bank can import → data portability

sections.heading: Computer Misuse Act 1990 (CMA)
sections.text: Why was it needed? In R v Gold and Schifreen (1988), two men got into BT's Prestel system with a password they had found. Their conviction was overturned because hacking was not a crime. The CMA closed the gap.

head: Section
Offence
Maximum sentence
rows: Unauthorised access to computer material
2 years
Unauthorised access with intent to commit a further crime
5 years
Unauthorised acts to impair a computer or data (e.g. malware, DoS)
10 years
3A (added 2006)
Making or supplying hacking tools
2 years
3ZA (added 2015)
Serious damage, e.g. to critical national infrastructure
14 years to life

points: Section 1 example: guessing a colleague's password to read their emails

sections.heading: Organisations' responsibility: due care
sections.text: The CMA makes the attacker a criminal. Organisations must exercise due care: reasonable steps to prevent unauthorised access, to meet their security duties under UK GDPR.
points: Access controls
Strong passwords + MFA
Disable leavers' accounts
Patch and update
Monitor and log access
Train staff; have clear policies
Apply it: Sam uses a colleague's password from a sticky note to change his sales figures
Sam has committed a CMA offence: unauthorised access and modification of data
The organisation failed in its due care (poor password practice, no training), a risk to GDPR integrity and confidentiality
So a hacked organisation can still be fined: it failed to keep data secure (due care)

sections.heading: Worked case study and exam technique
sections.text: ShopRight keeps full customer records long after orders are complete. It reuses delivery-update emails for marketing and ignores customers who ask it to stop. Old admin accounts are never disabled and systems are rarely patched. It is hacked. Use the method: Evidence → Responsibility → Control.

head: Evidence
Responsibility broken
Control to fix it
rows: "records long after orders are complete"
GDPR: storage limitation
Set a retention period; delete old records
"admin accounts never disabled … rarely patched"
CMA: failed in due care
Disable leavers' accounts; patch regularly
"reuses delivery-update emails for marketing"
GDPR: purpose limitation
Only market to people who opt in
"ignores customers who ask it to stop"
Right to object
Unsubscribe link; stop when asked

points: Identify / State: name it
Describe: say what it is or what happens
Explain: point + reason, linked to the scenario
Evaluate: both sides + a justified judgement
1 mark: "Storage limitation." (no explanation)
2 marks: "It breaches storage limitation (1) because it keeps customers' details forever, even after orders are delivered, so it holds data longer than needed (1)."

keyIdea: UK GDPR (with the DPA 2018) sets the rules for handling personal data: 7 principles, 6 lawful bases and 6 personal rights, enforced by the ICO. The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes breaking in a crime, and organisations must take due care to stop unauthorised access.
flashcards: Personal data (PII)
Any information that can identify a living person, on its own or combined with other data. PII = personally identifying information
UK GDPR + DPA 2018
The law that controls how organisations collect, store, use and share personal data, and gives people rights over their data
ICO
The Information Commissioner's Office: enforces UK GDPR, with fines up to £17.5m or 4% of turnover
Computer Misuse Act 1990 (CMA)
Makes it a crime to access or change computer material without permission
Lawfulness
GDPR principle: have a valid legal reason (lawful basis) to use the data
Fairness and transparency
GDPR principle: treat people fairly and be open about what is collected and why
Purpose limitation
GDPR principle: only use data for the purpose you told people (WHAT you do with it)
Accuracy
GDPR principle: keep data correct and up to date, and fix mistakes quickly
Data minimisation
GDPR principle: only collect data you actually need (HOW MUCH you collect)
Storage limitation
GDPR principle: don't keep data longer than needed
Integrity and confidentiality
GDPR principle: keep data secure from unauthorised access, loss or damage
Lawful basis
The legal reason for using personal data. Organisations must pick one of six before they start, and tell people
Consent
Lawful basis: the person has freely and clearly agreed. Must be a clear, active choice, not a pre-ticked box
Contractual obligation
Lawful basis: the data is needed to deliver a contract, e.g. bank details to take a monthly payment
Legitimate interest
Lawful basis: a genuine business reason that doesn't override people's rights, e.g. CCTV in a car park
Vital interest
Lawful basis: needed to protect someone's life, e.g. sharing allergy details with A&E
Legal requirement
Lawful basis: the law requires it, e.g. keeping staff right-to-work documents
Public interest
Lawful basis: needed for an official or public task, e.g. the DVLA issuing driving licences
Right of access
The right to see a copy of your data
Subject Access Request (SAR)
A request to an organisation to see a copy of the data it holds about you. It must usually respond within one month
Right to be informed
The right to be told how and why your data is used
Right to object
The right to say "stop", e.g. to direct marketing
Right to data portability
The right to get your data in a machine-readable format, e.g. to move to a new bank
Right not to be subject to automated decision-making
The right to ask for a human to review a decision made by a computer
R v Gold and Schifreen (1988)
Two men got into BT's Prestel system with a found password; their conviction was overturned because hacking wasn't a crime. This led to the CMA
CMA section 1
Unauthorised access to computer material. Up to 2 years
CMA section 2
Unauthorised access with intent to commit a further crime. Up to 5 years
CMA section 3
Unauthorised acts to impair a computer or data, e.g. malware or DoS. Up to 10 years
CMA sections 3A and 3ZA
3A (2006): making or supplying hacking tools, up to 2 years. 3ZA (2015): serious damage, e.g. to critical national infrastructure, 14 years to life
Due care
Reasonable steps an organisation takes to prevent unauthorised access, e.g. MFA, patching and disabling leavers' accounts

quiz.q: Which of these is personal data?
quiz.e: An IP address can help identify a living person, so it is personal data (PII).
The ICO enforces UK GDPR, with fines up to £17.5m or 4% of turnover.

quiz.q: A cinema asks for your National Insurance number to book a ticket. Which principle is breached?
quiz.e: It is collecting data it doesn't need to sell a ticket: data minimisation.

quiz.q: A school uses parents' emergency contact numbers to send fundraising texts. Which principle is breached?
quiz.e: The numbers were given for emergencies, not fundraising, so they are used for a different purpose.

quiz.q: A bank keeps writing to your old address after you told them you moved. Which principle is breached?
quiz.e: The data isn't kept correct and up to date: accuracy.

quiz.q: An unencrypted laptop of patient records is left on a train. Which principle is breached?
quiz.e: The data wasn't kept secure from unauthorised access or loss.

quiz.q: A shop keeps card details for years after orders are complete. Which principle is breached?
quiz.e: It keeps the data longer than needed.

quiz.q: What is the difference between purpose limitation and data minimisation?
o: Purpose limitation is about what you do with data; data minimisation is about how much you collect
Purpose limitation is about how long you keep data; data minimisation is about security
Data minimisation is a CMA offence
quiz.e: Purpose = WHAT you do with it. Minimisation = HOW MUCH you collect.

quiz.q: A gym takes your bank details to collect your monthly membership fee. Which lawful basis?
quiz.e: The data is needed to deliver the membership contract.

quiz.q: A school shares a pupil's allergy details with A&E. Which lawful basis?
quiz.e: It is needed to protect someone's life: vital interest.

quiz.q: Does a pre-ticked box count as consent?
o: Yes, if the box is clearly visible
No, consent must be a clear, active choice
quiz.e: Consent must be freely and clearly given, so the person has to actively choose.

quiz.q: A customer asks a company for a copy of all the data it holds about them. Which right are they using?
o: Right of access (a Subject Access Request)
quiz.e: Seeing a copy of your data is the right of access, through a Subject Access Request.

quiz.q: Priya asks her old bank for her history in a file her new bank can import. Which right?
quiz.e: Getting your data in a machine-readable format to move it is data portability.

quiz.q: How long do organisations usually have to respond to a rights request?
quiz.e: Organisations must usually respond within one month.

quiz.q: Why was the Computer Misuse Act 1990 needed?
o: To give people rights over their data
To fine companies that lose data
In R v Gold and Schifreen, hacking wasn't a crime, so the convictions were overturned
quiz.e: The CMA closed the gap by making unauthorised access a crime.

quiz.q: Spreading malware to impair a computer is an offence under which section of the CMA?
quiz.e: Section 3 covers unauthorised acts to impair a computer or data, e.g. malware or DoS (up to 10 years).

quiz.q: Why could an organisation that was hacked still be fined?
o: It failed to keep data secure (due care)
Because the hacker can't be found
Organisations are always fined after a hack
Because it broke the CMA itself
quiz.e: Organisations must take due care to stop unauthorised access. Failing to do so breaks GDPR integrity and confidentiality.

apply.title: Which principle, basis or right?
apply.intro: Read each scenario, underline the evidence in your head, then pick the best answer.

items.task: A quiz app secretly copies users' phone contacts.
items.e: It isn't open about what it collects: fairness and transparency.

items.task: A recruitment agency keeps rejected applicants' CVs for 15 years.
items.e: It keeps data far longer than needed.

items.task: A fitness app shares users' location history with advertisers, with no lawful basis.
items.e: There is no valid legal reason to use the data this way.

items.task: A college uses CCTV in its car park to keep people safe.
items.e: A genuine reason that doesn't override people's rights: legitimate interest.

items.task: An employer keeps staff right-to-work documents.
The DVLA uses driver details to issue driving licences.
items.e: It is an official, public task.

items.task: A photographer asks parents' permission before posting school play photos.
items.e: The parents freely and clearly agree.

items.task: A customer tells an online shop to stop sending them marketing emails.
items.e: Saying "stop" to direct marketing is the right to object.

items.task: An algorithm turns down Leo's loan application. He asks for a person to check it.
o: Right not to be subject to automated decision-making
items.e: Asking for a human to review a computer's decision.

items.task: Amira leaves a social network and asks it to delete all her posts.
o: Right to have data corrected, removed or restricted
items.e: Deleting data falls under corrected, removed or restricted.

items.task: An employee guesses a colleague's password to read their emails.
items.e: Unauthorised access to computer material is a section 1 offence.

items.task: Sam uses a password from a sticky note to change his sales figures. What has the ORGANISATION failed to do?
o: Respond to a Subject Access Request
Take due care, e.g. good password practice and staff training
items.e: Sam committed a CMA offence; the organisation failed in its due care, a risk to GDPR integrity and confidentiality.

pts: Any information that can identify a living person
on its own or combined with other data, e.g. a name, address or IP address
exam.tip: Say it identifies a LIVING person, and mention that combined data counts too.

exam.sc: SnapPrint, an online photo printer, asks customers for their name, address, email and date of birth. It keeps all photos and details forever, even after orders are delivered.
exam.q: 2. Explain one way SnapPrint has breached UK GDPR.
pts: It breaches storage limitation / data minimisation
because it keeps details forever even after orders are delivered, so it holds data longer than needed / because a date of birth isn't needed to print photos
exam.tip: Name the principle, then say "because…" with evidence from the scenario. A name on its own only gets 1 mark.

exam.sc: A gym takes members' bank details so it can collect their monthly membership fee.
exam.q: 3. Identify the lawful basis the gym is using and explain why it applies.
pts: Contractual obligation
because the bank details are needed to deliver the membership contract by taking the monthly payment
exam.tip: Don't assume consent: it is only 1 of 6 bases.

exam.sc: Brightway Tutoring is an online tutoring company. When parents sign up, it asks for their name, email, home address, date of birth and National Insurance number. It keeps every family's records for ten years after lessons stop. It has started sending parents adverts for a partner's summer camps, using the email addresses they gave for lesson reminders.
exam.q: 4(a). Identify two GDPR principles Brightway has breached.
pts: One of: data minimisation (a National Insurance number / date of birth isn't needed) or storage limitation (records kept for ten years)
A second, e.g. purpose limitation (emails given for lesson reminders are used for adverts)
exam.tip: "Identify" needs names only, but each must match evidence in the scenario.

exam.sc: Brightway Tutoring is an online tutoring company. When parents sign up, it asks for their name, email, home address, date of birth and National Insurance number. It keeps every family's records for ten years after lessons stop. It has started sending parents adverts for a partner's summer camps, using the email addresses they gave for lesson reminders.
exam.q: 4(b). Explain how reusing parents' emails breaches UK GDPR.
pts: It breaches purpose limitation
because the emails were given only for lesson reminders but are being used for adverts
It may also lack a lawful basis / consent for marketing
because parents did not clearly opt in to receive adverts from a partner company
exam.tip: Two linked points: principle + because + scenario evidence, twice.

exam.sc: Brightway Tutoring is an online tutoring company. When parents sign up, it asks for their name, email, home address, date of birth and National Insurance number. It keeps every family's records for ten years after lessons stop. It has started sending parents adverts for a partner's summer camps, using the email addresses they gave for lesson reminders.
exam.q: 4(c). Suggest two practical controls Brightway should put in place.
pts: Set a retention period and delete old records
so data isn't kept longer than needed (storage limitation)
Only send marketing to parents who actively opt in, with an unsubscribe link
so emails are only used for the purpose agreed and people can object
exam.tip: For each control, say what to do and which problem it fixes.

exam.sc: A patient emails Dr Patel's small medical clinic asking for a copy of all the information it holds about them. The clinic ignores the email for three months. Staff share one login to the records system, and the password is written on a sticky note next to the reception computer.
exam.q: 5(a). Identify the right the patient is using.
pts: Right of access (a Subject Access Request)
exam.tip: The verb is "see a copy", so it is access.

exam.sc: A patient emails Dr Patel's small medical clinic asking for a copy of all the information it holds about them. The clinic ignores the email for three months. Staff share one login to the records system, and the password is written on a sticky note next to the reception computer.
exam.q: 5(b). Explain two ways the clinic has failed its legal responsibilities.
pts: It ignored the request for three months
when it must usually respond within one month, so it failed the patient's right of access
Staff share one login with the password on a sticky note
so it has failed in its due care to stop unauthorised access, putting the integrity and confidentiality of medical records at risk
exam.tip: Use both pieces of evidence: one about rights, one about security.

exam.q: 6. Explain why an organisation that is hacked could still be fined.
pts: It may have failed in its due care / not kept data secure
which breaks the GDPR principle of integrity and confidentiality, so the ICO can fine it
exam.tip: The attacker breaks the CMA, but the organisation is judged on whether it took reasonable steps.

exam.sc: Sam uses a colleague's password from a sticky note to log in and change his sales figures.
exam.q: 7. Explain which law Sam has broken.
pts: The Computer Misuse Act 1990
because he accessed and changed data without permission (unauthorised access and modification)
exam.tip: Name the law, then link it to what Sam actually did.
